prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B001) because it is the field I know best, but on reflection the optical lattice clock (B048) is the strongest case before us, and every member ranked it in their top three. That breadth is not itself a merit argument. The merit argument is independent: the magic-wavelength idea is a clean, original invention; Ye's group pushed it to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18; it is reproduced by many laboratories and underpins tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. The credited pair maps well onto concept (Katori) and record-setting realisation (Ye), which gives a cleaner attribution than any other shortlisted entry, including my own first choice. Because the 2025 prize has just recognised macroscopic quantum phenomena in superconducting circuits, choosing a precision-measurement achievement in atomic physics also spreads recognition across fields in a way I find defensible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial overlap with the 2005 prize on the optical frequency comb (Hall and Haensch), and the contributions of other clock groups (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom) fall outside the supplied names, so a two-person award is a judgment on credit and not a settled partition. A second concern is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so one could argue the capstone is still ahead. I judge the weighting of Katori versus Ye from general knowledge, not from verified records.

responses.point: Ranked B048 first because the atomic structure and systematic-shift physics are secure, and placed B001 last because its closeness to the 2025 prize reduces timeliness.
responses.response: I now largely agree on both counts. Your point on systematic shifts, with independent labs reaching the 1e-18 level and routine intercomparisons, is what persuades me the lattice clock is mature and not merely popular. On B001 I accept your timeliness argument: my own opening rank 1 for circuit QED rested partly on subject familiarity, and the 2025 prize makes a near-term second superconducting-circuit award hard to defend. The field is not scientifically weaker, only less well timed.

responses.point: Put topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (B019) first, valuing how the concept translated into material-specific predictions confirmed by experiment.
responses.response: I agree B019 is an outstanding concept with extensive confirmation, and I rank it as my first alternative. Where I differ is attribution: the supplied credit leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe prediction directly enabled the Molenkamp observation, and also Fu and Moore on the three-dimensional side. You acknowledge this, but I think it is more than a footnote, since a prize that must leave out the HgTe prediction rewards an incomplete chain. The related 2016 topology prize also narrows the novelty. For those reasons I place it second to B048.

responses.point: Ranked B048 first as the cleanest case of precision opening new science, and ranked trapped-ion logic (B003) third as overdue relative to its impact.
responses.response: I share your reading of B048 and your view that B003 is highly mature. On B003 I would qualify the 'overdue' claim: the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems already honoured Wineland, and Monroe and other ion groups have experimental claims that Blatt does not cover. The Cirac-Zoller theory is outstanding, but a theory-plus-one-experimentalist trio will draw dispute over who is left out. I keep B003 as a serious second alternative rather than the preferred choice, and note that Zoller also appears in B021, which could split support.

responses.point: Ranked the Higgs discovery with ATLAS and CMS (B054) first as a foundational result, with the most defensible configuration being the leaders of the two detectors.
responses.response: The scientific importance of the Higgs discovery is not in doubt, and the 2013 prize left the experimental completion unrecognised. My difficulty is attribution: a collaboration of several thousand people, with Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti each having strong claims, makes any three-person list contestable in a way the clock pair is not. Also, only three members ranked it at all, so it is not a broad committee view. I would not oppose it in a later prize, but I do not see it displacing B048 now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 frequency-comb prize as a substantial overlap with the lattice clock.
How to weigh Katori's concept against Ye's development, and whether other clock pioneers outside the supplied names should alter the configuration.
Whether waiting for the SI second redefinition would give a better-framed citation, or whether timing is already right.
How much of my movement away from B001 reflects genuine reconsideration given my subject-matter closeness to circuit QED.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue for B001 (circuit QED): I am a circuit and waveguide QED theorist and director of WACQT at Chalmers, with documented connections to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum; Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. My profile shows no specific connection to the B048 candidates (Katori, Ye), so none is apparent there.
